title: Fossils: Clues from Long Ago
summary: What fossils are, how they form in layers of rock, how scientists dig them up and date them, and what they tell us about the past, including the Nafud desert in Saudi Arabia.
poll: A fossil can tell us more about the past than an old book can.

versions.title: Clues in Rock
versions.text:
See this rock? It has a shell in it. It is a fossil. A fossil is a clue from long ago.

A fossil is left from a plant or an animal. It is kept in rock. It can be a bone. It can be a tooth. It can be a shell. It can be a foot print.

How does a fossil form? An animal dies. Mud falls on it. Sand falls on it. Now it is buried. The soft parts rot. The hard parts stay. More mud piles on top. Each pile is a layer. The mud turns to rock. This takes a long, long time.

Some people dig them up. They use small tools. They use soft brushes. They work with care.

Deep rock is old. Top rock is new. So a deep fossil is the old one.

They tell us a lot. Shells are found on hills. So the sea was there once! In Saudi Arabia, there is a big desert. It is the Nafud. Fossil bones of hippos are there. Hippos need lakes. So the land was once green and wet.

versions.text:

A fossil is what is left of a plant or an animal that lived long ago. It is kept safe in rock. Some fossils are bones, teeth, or shells. Some are foot prints that an animal left in mud.

versions.title: Fossils: Clues from the Past
versions.text:
Have you ever found a rock with the shape of a shell inside it? You may have found a fossil. Fossils are clues that help us learn about life long ago.

A fossil is the remains or the mark of a plant or an animal that lived a long time ago. It has been kept safe inside rock. Many fossils are bones, teeth, or shells. Some are footprints that an animal left in soft mud.

How does a fossil form? First, an animal dies near water. Soon, mud or sand covers it, and it is buried. The soft parts of the body rot away, but the hard parts, such as bones, stay. Then more mud piles up on top, one layer after another. Over a very long time, the heavy layers press down and turn into rock.

Scientists who study fossils dig them out slowly. They use small picks and soft brushes so the old bones do not crack.

Layers of rock help tell the age of a fossil. The deep layers formed first, so they are the oldest. A fossil found deep down is usually older than one near the top.

Fossils show us how the world has changed. Sea shells have been found on high hills, so the sea once covered that land. In the Nafud desert in Saudi Arabia, scientists found fossil bones of hippos and elephants. Hippos need lakes and rivers, so this dry desert was once green and wet.

versions.title: Fossils: Clues from the Past
versions.text:
Imagine cracking open a rock and finding the shape of a shell inside. You would be holding a fossil. Fossils are clues that help us learn about plants and animals that lived long before people.

A fossil is the preserved remains or the mark of a living thing from long ago. Many fossils are hard body parts, such as bones, teeth, and shells. Others are signs that an animal left behind, such as footprints pressed into soft mud. Many fossils come from animals that are now extinct. That means none of them are still alive.

Most fossils form in a few steps. First, an animal dies near a lake, river, or sea. Soon, mud or sand covers its body, and it is buried. This mud and sand is called sediment. The soft parts rot away, but the hard parts, such as bones, remain. Next, more sediment piles up on top, one layer after another. Over a very long time, the weight of the layers presses the mud into rock. Water in the ground also carries minerals into the bones and slowly turns them to stone.

A scientist who studies fossils is called a paleontologist. Paleontologists dig with great care. They use small picks and soft brushes so the old bones do not break.

The layers of rock also help them tell how old a fossil is. Deep layers formed first, so they are usually the oldest. A fossil found deep down is usually older than one near the top.

Fossils show how much the world has changed. Sea shells have been found high on hills, so the sea once covered that land. In the Nafud desert in Saudi Arabia, scientists found fossil bones of hippos and elephants. Since hippos need lakes and rivers, this dry desert must once have been green and wet.

versions.title: Fossils: Clues from Long Ago
versions.text:
Imagine splitting open a rock and discovering the delicate outline of a shell inside. You would be holding a fossil, a clue that has remained hidden in the ground for thousands or even millions of years. A fossil is the preserved remains or trace of an organism from the distant past. Many fossils are hard body parts, such as bones, teeth, and shells. Others are traces that an animal left behind, including footprints and burrows pressed into soft mud. A large proportion of fossils belong to species that are now extinct, meaning that no living members of their kind survive today.

Most fossils develop through a series of stages. First, an animal dies near a lake, river, or sea. Mud or sand, known as sediment, rapidly covers its body. The soft tissues decay, but the hard parts remain. Gradually, additional sediment accumulates in layers, and the tremendous weight of these layers compresses the lower ones into solid rock. Meanwhile, groundwater seeping through the sediment carries dissolved minerals into the bones, slowly replacing the original material and transforming it into stone.

A scientist who studies fossils is called a paleontologist. Paleontologists work patiently, using small picks and soft brushes so that fragile specimens do not crack.

Rock layers also help paleontologists estimate the age of a fossil. The deepest layers usually formed first, so a fossil buried far below the surface is generally older than one located near the top.

versions.title: Fossils: Clues from Long Ago
versions.text:
Imagine splitting open a rock and discovering the delicate outline of an ancient shell inside. You would be holding a fossil, a piece of evidence that has remained concealed underground for thousands or even millions of years. Fossils allow scientists to investigate organisms that existed long before human beings appeared.

A fossil is the preserved remains or trace of an organism from the distant past. Many fossils consist of hard body parts, such as bones, teeth, and shells. Others are traces that an animal left behind, including footprints and burrows impressed into soft mud. A considerable proportion of fossils belong to species that are now extinct, meaning that no living members of their kind survive anywhere on Earth.

Most fossils develop through a predictable sequence of stages. First, an animal dies near a lake, river, or sea, and mud or sand, known as sediment, rapidly covers its body. The soft tissues decay, but the hard parts remain. Gradually, additional sediment accumulates in horizontal layers, and the tremendous weight of these layers compresses the lower ones into solid rock. Meanwhile, groundwater seeping through the sediment carries dissolved minerals into the bones, slowly replacing the original material and transforming it into stone.

A scientist who specializes in fossils is called a paleontologist. Paleontologists excavate patiently, using small picks and delicate brushes so that fragile specimens do not crack or crumble.

Rock layers also help paleontologists estimate the age of a fossil. The deepest layers generally formed first, so a fossil buried far beneath the surface is usually older than one located near the top.

Fossils reveal how dramatically our planet has transformed. Marine shells have been discovered high on hillsides, demonstrating that an ocean once covered that territory. In the Nafud desert of Saudi Arabia, paleontologists uncovered fossil bones of hippos and elephants. Because hippos depend on permanent lakes and rivers, this arid desert must once have been considerably greener and wetter.

versions.title: Fossils: Evidence from Long Ago
versions.text:
Imagine splitting open an ordinary rock and discovering the delicate outline of an ancient shell inside it. You would be holding a fossil, a piece of evidence that has remained concealed underground for thousands or even millions of years. Because fossils preserve information about organisms that existed long before human beings appeared, they function as an extraordinary record of the history of life on Earth.

A fossil is the preserved remains or trace of an organism from the distant past. Many fossils consist of durable body parts, such as bones, teeth, and shells, while others are traces that an animal left behind, including footprints and burrows imprinted in soft mud. A considerable proportion of fossils belong to species that are now extinct, which means that no living members of their kind survive anywhere on the planet.

Most fossils develop through a predictable sequence of stages. Initially, an animal dies near a lake, river, or sea, and mud or sand, collectively known as sediment, rapidly buries its body. The soft tissues decompose, whereas the hard parts remain intact. Gradually, additional sediment accumulates in horizontal layers, and the tremendous weight of these layers compresses the lower ones into solid rock. Simultaneously, groundwater seeping through the sediment deposits dissolved minerals inside the bones, progressively replacing the original material and transforming it into stone.

A scientist who specializes in investigating fossils is called a paleontologist. Paleontologists excavate patiently and methodically, using small picks and delicate brushes so that fragile specimens do not fracture or crumble before they can be examined.

Rock layers also help paleontologists estimate the age of a fossil. Since the deepest layers generally formed earliest, a fossil buried far beneath the surface is usually considerably older than one located near the top.

Fossils reveal how dramatically our planet has transformed over time. Marine shells have been discovered high on hillsides, demonstrating that an ocean once covered that territory. In the Nafud desert of Saudi Arabia, paleontologists uncovered fossil bones of hippos and elephants. Because hippos depend on permanent lakes and rivers, this arid desert must once have been considerably greener and wetter than it is today.

versions.title: Fossils: Evidence from the Distant Past
versions.text:
Imagine splitting open an ordinary rock and discovering the delicate outline of an ancient shell embedded inside it. You would be holding a fossil, a piece of evidence that has remained concealed underground for thousands or even millions of years. Because fossils preserve information about organisms that existed long before human beings appeared, they function as an extraordinary archive documenting the history of life on our planet.

A fossil is the preserved remains or trace of an organism from the distant past. Many fossils consist of durable body parts, such as bones, teeth, and shells, while others are traces that an animal left behind, including footprints and burrows imprinted in once-soft mud. A considerable proportion of fossils represent species that are now extinct, which means that no living members of their kind survive anywhere on Earth.

Most fossils develop through a relatively predictable sequence of stages. Initially, an animal dies near a lake, river, or sea, and mud or sand, collectively described as sediment, rapidly buries its body before scavengers can scatter it. The soft tissues decompose, whereas the more resistant hard parts remain intact. Gradually, additional sediment accumulates in horizontal layers, and the tremendous weight of these overlying layers compresses the lower ones into solid rock. Simultaneously, groundwater percolating through the sediment deposits dissolved minerals inside the bones, progressively replacing the original material and transforming it into stone.

A scientist who specializes in investigating fossils is called a paleontologist. Paleontologists excavate patiently and methodically, using small picks and delicate brushes so that fragile specimens do not fracture or disintegrate before they can be thoroughly examined.

Rock layers additionally help paleontologists estimate the approximate age of a fossil. Since the deepest layers generally formed earliest, a fossil buried far beneath the surface is usually considerably older than one located near the top.

Fossils reveal how dramatically our planet has transformed across immense periods of time. Marine shells have been discovered high on hillsides, demonstrating that an ocean once covered that territory. In the Nafud desert of Saudi Arabia, paleontologists uncovered fossil bones of hippos and elephants. Because hippos depend on permanent lakes and rivers, this arid desert must once have been considerably greener and wetter than it is today.

versions.title: Fossils: Evidence from the Distant Past
versions.text:
Imagine splitting open an ordinary rock and discovering the delicate outline of an ancient shell embedded inside it. You would be holding a fossil, a piece of evidence that has remained concealed underground for thousands or even millions of years. Because fossils preserve information about organisms that existed long before human beings appeared, they function as an extraordinary archive documenting the history of life on our planet, and they allow scientists to reconstruct environments that no person ever witnessed.

A fossil is the preserved remains or trace of an organism from the distant past. Many fossils consist of durable anatomical structures, such as bones, teeth, and shells, while others are traces that an animal left behind, including footprints and burrows imprinted in once-soft mud. A considerable proportion of fossils represent species that are now extinct, which means that no living representatives of their kind survive anywhere on Earth.

Most fossils develop through a relatively predictable sequence of stages. Initially, an animal dies near a lake, river, or sea, and mud or sand, collectively described as sediment, rapidly buries its body before scavengers can scatter the remains. The soft tissues decompose, whereas the more resistant mineralized parts remain intact. Gradually, additional sediment accumulates in horizontal layers, and the tremendous weight of these overlying deposits compresses the lower ones into solid sedimentary rock. Simultaneously, groundwater percolating through the sediment deposits dissolved minerals inside the bones, progressively replacing the original material and ultimately transforming it into stone.

A scientist who specializes in investigating fossils is called a paleontologist. Paleontologists excavate patiently and methodically, employing small picks and delicate brushes so that fragile specimens do not fracture or disintegrate before they can be thoroughly documented and examined in a laboratory.

Rock layers additionally enable paleontologists to estimate the approximate age of a fossil. Since the deepest layers generally accumulated earliest, a fossil buried far beneath the surface is usually considerably older than one located near the top, a principle that geologists describe as superposition.

Fossils reveal how dramatically our planet has transformed across immense periods of geological time. Marine shells have been discovered high on mountainsides, demonstrating that an ocean once submerged that territory. In the Nafud desert of Saudi Arabia, paleontologists uncovered fossilized bones of hippos and elephants. Because hippos depend on permanent lakes and rivers, this arid desert must once have been considerably greener and wetter than it is today, which illustrates how dramatically regional climates can fluctuate.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to clean old bones
What fossils are and what they teach us
Why hippos still live in the desert today
How to make a rock at home
questions.why: Each part of the article tells what a fossil is, how it forms in rock, and what it shows about the past.

wrong.A: The article tells how people dig up fossils, not how to clean bones.
wrong.C: Hippos do not live in the desert today. Their old bones show the land was once wet.
wrong.D: The article tells how rock forms in nature over a long time, not at home.

They turn into a shell.
They float up to the top.
They stay soft for a long time.

wrong.C: Nothing in the article says the soft parts float.
wrong.D: The article says the soft parts rot. Only hard parts last.

wrong.B: The article does not say people wash fossils with soap.
wrong.C: The article names tools and brushes, not bare hands.

questions.stem: Read: "More mud piles on top. Each pile is a layer." What is a layer?

A kind of bone from an animal
One part on top of another
A soft brush

wrong.A: A layer piles up. It is not a hole.
wrong.B: Bones are buried under the layers, but a layer is not a bone.
wrong.D: Brushes are tools. A layer is part of the ground.

questions.stem: Shells have been found high on hills. What does this tell us?

Hills grow shells every year.

wrong.C: Hills do not grow shells. The shells are fossils from long ago.
wrong.D: The shells are fossils in the rock, not things people dropped.

questions.stem: Why do fossil diggers most likely work slowly and with care?

They want to sleep in the desert.
Fossils are very hot.
They do not know where to dig.

wrong.B: Nothing in the article is about sleeping in the desert.
wrong.C: The article never says fossils are hot.
wrong.D: Working with care is about keeping fossils safe, not about not knowing where to dig.

questions.stem: An animal dies and is buried. Mud piles on top in layers. What happens next?
options: The animal wakes up.
The mud blows away.
The mud turns to rock.
The bones turn back into soft parts.

wrong.B: The mud stays and piles up. It does not blow away.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell about hippo bones in the Nafud desert?

To say hippos still live there now
To tell people not to visit the desert
To show the desert was once green and wet

wrong.B: The bones are fossils from long ago. Hippos do not live there now.

LOW.prompt: Tell how a fossil forms. Use the words first, next, and last.
checklist: I told the steps in the right order.
I used first, next, and last.
I used at least two words from the article, such as buried or layer.
LOW.modelAnswer: First, an animal dies and gets buried under mud or sand. Next, the soft parts of its body rot away, but the hard parts like bones stay and get covered by more layers over time. Last, minerals slowly turn the buried bones into a hard fossil inside the rock. This is how scientists found fossil bones even in a dry desert like the Nafud.

MID.prompt: Explain how rock layers help a paleontologist tell the age of a fossil. Use details from the article.
checklist: I explained which layers are older and why.
I used at least two details from the article.
I used at least two key words correctly.
MID.modelAnswer: Rock layers help a paleontologist tell the age of a fossil because of the order in which the layers of sediment formed. The deepest layers were buried first, so a fossil preserved deep underground is usually older than one found closer to the surface. Over time, minerals carried by water slowly replace parts of the buried bones, turning them to stone, which is one detail that shows how long the process can take. Many fossils even belong to animals that are now extinct, so studying which layer they came from helps scientists understand how long ago those creatures lived.

wrong.C: The bones are replaced by stone, not simply dissolved away.
wrong.D: The article says the soft tissues decay.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a trace fossil described in the article?
options: A tooth
A shell
A leg bone
A burrow
questions.why: The article says traces an animal left behind include footprints and burrows.

wrong.A: A tooth is a hard body part, not a trace.
wrong.B: A shell is a body part of the animal.
wrong.C: A bone is part of the animal's body, not a trace it left.

questions.stem: The article calls the Nafud an arid desert. What does arid mean?
options: Sandy and windy
Large and flat
Very dry
Hot at night
questions.why: The article contrasts the arid desert with a time when it was greener and wetter, so arid means very dry.

wrong.A: Deserts can be sandy, but arid refers to dryness.
wrong.B: Arid does not describe size or shape.
wrong.D: Arid is about lack of water, not temperature.

questions.stem: Why do paleontologists most likely use delicate brushes instead of large tools?
options: Large tools are too expensive.
Fragile specimens could crack.
Brushes help them find older layers faster.
Brushes add minerals to the bones.
questions.why: The article says they work patiently so that fragile specimens do not crack or crumble.

wrong.C: Brushes protect fossils; they do not speed up digging.
wrong.D: Minerals come from groundwater, not brushes.

questions.stem: Marine shells are found high on a hillside. What does this suggest about the rock of that hill?
options: It formed from sediment under the sea.
It was carried there by people long ago.
It is younger than the shells inside it.
It formed from melted lava.
questions.why: The article says such shells show that an ocean once covered the land, so the rock formed from sediment under the sea.

wrong.B: The article treats the shells as natural evidence, not something people moved.
wrong.C: The shells were buried as the rock formed, so the rock is not younger than them.
wrong.D: The article explains fossils form in sediment, not lava.

questions.stem: What causes the lower layers of sediment to become solid rock?
options: Hot sunlight drying the surface
Animals packing the mud with their feet
The weight of the layers above
Paleontologists pressing on the ground
questions.why: The article says the tremendous weight of the layers compresses the lower ones into rock.

wrong.A: The article does not say sunlight forms the rock.
wrong.B: Footprints are traces, but animals do not turn layers into rock.
wrong.D: Paleontologists dig fossils out; they do not make rock.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the example of hippo and elephant fossils in the Nafud desert?
options: To argue that hippos should return to Saudi Arabia
To explain how paleontologists use brushes
To compare hippos with elephants
To show how fossils reveal a changed environment
questions.why: The example shows how fossils prove that a dry desert in Saudi Arabia was once greener and wetter.

wrong.A: The author makes no such argument.
wrong.B: Tools are explained in a different paragraph.
wrong.C: The two animals are not compared.

HIGH.prompt: Some people say fossils are the best evidence we have about the distant past. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that fossils are some of the best evidence we have about the distant past, because they reveal facts about ancient organisms that no other record can show. When paleontologists carefully excavate fossils that were long concealed underground, the layers of sediment that compress around them reveal roughly how old each fossil is, since deeper layers formed earlier than those nearer the surface. Even more strikingly, fossil bones of hippos and elephants found in the arid Nafud desert prove that this now-dry region was once green and filled with lakes and rivers, since hippos cannot survive without that kind of environment. Because fossils can reveal both the age of ancient life and the climate conditions those organisms needed to survive, I think they remain one of our most powerful windows into Earth's distant past.
